stims.text: AI fluency means collaborating effectively, efficiently, ethically, and safely. Delegation concerns choosing and distributing work; Description communicates the desired product, approach, and interaction; Discernment evaluates what happens; Diligence concerns responsible choices, transparency, and accountability. These competencies work together across automation, augmentation, and agency. A useful output is only part of a successful collaboration. Decisions about the work, communication, evaluation, and responsibility address different needs; the framework helps identify which need requires attention. The competencies interact and can recur throughout the work rather than forming a required one-pass sequence.

Distinguish Automation, where AI executes a specified task; Augmentation, where human and AI develop the work through collaboration; and Agency, where AI is configured to act independently on someone’s behalf. Choose a mode according to how settled the desired outcome is and how the work should involve human participation. A project may combine modes. Executing a known request and exploring an unsettled problem require different kinds of participation. Independent ongoing action introduces a different arrangement again. No mode is inherently best for every situation.

Generative AI creates new content, whereas the contrasting classification example assigns existing material to categories. An LLM is a generative model trained to predict and generate language using learned parameters. A generated answer is not necessarily a prewritten or verified answer retrieved from a database. The distinction helps explain why one assistant can draft many kinds of content and why a fluent answer still needs evaluation. A language assistant may also use retrieval tools; distinguish information obtained through tools from generation based on learned patterns.

In the course’s account, modern generative AI was enabled jointly by architectural and algorithmic developments, large digital datasets, and increased computing power. Scaling describes empirical improvements associated with more model capacity, data, and computation, including newly observed capabilities. It does not establish that a larger model will be correct on every individual task. Data provides training material, architectures organize processing and learning, and computation makes training feasible. Their joint role explains why any one ingredient alone is an incomplete account.

Distinguish pre-training, which develops predictive patterns from training examples; subsequent training, which shapes instruction-following and other behavior; and inference, which generates a response from learned patterns and the available prompt. Responding to a new message is different from those training stages. The distinction connects the model’s learned behavior with its present input. It explains why a response can adapt to a request without being a stored answer or evidence that a new training run occurred.

Instructions and examples in the current context can guide an LLM to a new task without additional model training. When an immediate task is poorly specified or its pattern is unclear, consider improving those instructions or examples. A change in conversational behavior alone does not demonstrate retraining of the underlying model. The current prompt supplies task-specific information that the model can use alongside its learned patterns. That makes conversational guidance a practical way to adapt its work during use. Use relevant instructions or demonstrations to clarify the immediate task.

Distinguish the model’s training cutoff from information it can obtain through supplied material and available tools. A request about recent events or private records may require access beyond learned knowledge. Determine what relevant information is actually available instead of assuming that a capable assistant can access it. A cutoff limits innate knowledge of later events, while tools and provided documents can supply additional evidence. Neither general capability nor web access automatically provides access to a private data source. Better wording does not by itself grant missing information or tool access.

Generated responses can contain confident factual errors, including inaccuracies learned from training material and mistakes in combining information. Fluent wording and expressed confidence are insufficient evidence that an important claim is correct. Evaluate the claim using relevant knowledge and evidence. Training does not verify every source fact, and generating plausible text is different from establishing truth. This is why even convincing responses remain subject to human judgment.

An assistant can process only a finite amount of conversational information at once, including user messages, its responses, and supplied content. Do not assume that earlier or oversized material remains available merely because it once appeared in the conversation; reason about what information the current task needs. When relevant information falls outside the usable context, it cannot simply continue to guide the response. Context limits can therefore affect work with long documents and extended conversations. Reason about finite usable context without assuming one universal truncation or memory mechanism.

Repeated requests can produce different outputs because generation involves probabilistic choices. This variability can help generate alternatives but complicates consistency. Some interfaces expose a temperature control; its availability must not be assumed. Different wording is not, by itself, evidence of better accuracy. A process that can select among plausible continuations can yield variation across attempts. The value of that variation depends on whether the task needs exploration or consistent results.

Multi-step mathematical and logical reasoning can fail, even as reasoning and extended-thinking models improve. Some models already work through steps by default. Interpret an answer’s reasoning quality using the actual task and observable work rather than assuming either guaranteed success or a universal need for a step-by-step prompt. Improved reasoning capability and remaining fallibility can coexist. Whether extra guidance is useful depends partly on what the assistant already does and what the task requires.

Before deciding how to involve AI, clarify the desired outcome, why it matters, what success would look like, and the work needed. Distinguish routine work, uncertainty that calls for exploration, missing information, and demands for critical judgment. Without a clear goal and understanding of the work, it is difficult to choose a useful AI contribution, evaluate the output, or recognize when human intervention is needed.

Develop task-specific knowledge of available AI systems through relevant hands-on comparisons. Consider their capabilities, limitations, access, and tradeoffs, and revise choices as systems and needs change. Do not assume that one assistant is best for every kind of work. Different systems can perform differently on the work that matters to the user, and those capabilities evolve. Practical comparison connects platform choice to the actual task. Compare systems using relevant task outcomes and requirements; no single task comparison establishes a universal ranking.

Break work into meaningful tasks and allocate each to human work, AI execution, joint exploration, or independent AI action according to the goal, available capabilities, and need for human expertise and judgment. Reconsider the allocation when the work reveals a poor fit. Human and AI contributions have complementary strengths. Allocating each part according to those strengths can be more useful than treating maximum automation as the goal.

Specify the desired output, its audience and purpose, and the requirements that make it usable. Include relevant format, length, style, scope, and other constraints rather than leaving the assistant to guess what success means. Clear product requirements connect the assistant’s response to the intended use and give the user concrete criteria for judging it. Specify constraints relevant to the task rather than mechanically repeating a fixed checklist.

Supply relevant background, the reason for the request, the user’s knowledge level, and task-specific information that the assistant does not already have. The user’s situation can differ from the assistant’s available context; supplying that information reduces the need to guess about the audience, purpose, and constraints. Relevant background changes the level, scope, and constraints that a useful answer must address; the assistant cannot simply infer the user’s unstated situation. Supply information that changes what a suitable answer should contain, rather than unrelated background.

Guide the workflow, sources, sequence, or analytical method when successful execution depends on a particular approach, especially when the user has relevant domain knowledge the assistant lacks. Detailed steps are not necessary for every straightforward task, and reasoning models may already perform steps by default. There can be several reasonable ways to execute a request. Describing a required method conveys the user’s task-specific expertise and helps align the approach with the intended work. Distinguish specifying the required task method from merely requesting an explanation of an answer.

Specify the kind of conversational partner needed: exploration or convergence, challenge or support, brevity or detail, and a useful role, perspective, style, or tone. Judge whether the resulting interaction actually serves the task. The same task can call for different kinds of engagement. Stating the desired behavior helps align the interaction with the user’s needs rather than leaving it generic. Choose the desired behavior to fit the present task and stage of work.

Try a clear instruction first when it may suffice. When a desired pattern is difficult to describe or the response misses it, provide examples that actually demonstrate the intended transformation or output and cover relevant variation. Examples show a pattern for the assistant to emulate; they are not required for every task. Demonstrations can communicate a particular pattern more concretely than an abstract instruction, especially when the user can recognize the desired style more easily than describe it. Choose correct input–output demonstrations and relevant variation without requiring a fixed number of examples.

For a suitable task and an assistant that does not already deliberate by default, an instruction to consider factors, constraints, and alternative approaches before answering may help. Distinguish guidance before completing the work from asking for an explanation afterward. Extra deliberation instructions are not universally necessary or beneficial. Making room for consideration before completing a task differs from asking for an explanation after completion; reasoning or extended-thinking models may already do the former by default. A later explanation does not by itself change the already-produced answer.

When unsure how to formulate a useful request, explain the actual goal and the difficulty to the assistant and ask it to help clarify or improve the prompt. Check whether its proposed wording still represents the user’s intended need. Request formulation can itself be a collaborative task, so the user need not already know ideal wording to begin.

Evaluate the output against the actual task: factual accuracy, audience and purpose fit, coherence, requirements, and practical value. Use relevant domain knowledge to decide what to retain, revise, or discard. Polished prose or one successful quality dimension is not enough to establish overall suitability. An answer can be accurate yet unusable for the intended audience or purpose. Product discernment connects the result to what the user actually needs. Use the stated brief and relevant evidence rather than accepting the assistant’s confident presentation as verification.

Evaluate the assistant’s observable work for logical errors, lost constraints, unsuitable steps, fixation, circularity, and reintroduction of rejected material. Identify the step or pattern that conflicts with the agreed approach, particularly when the final answer is difficult to judge directly. A fluent result can conceal a drift away from the intended method. Following the observable work helps detect that mismatch and provides something specific to correct. Use the visible work and conversation as evidence when evaluating process.

Evaluate whether the assistant communicates at a useful level, responds to feedback and direction, asks helpful questions, and supports an efficient interaction. Identify behavioral mismatches separately from errors in the output or the work method. Good work can still be difficult to use when communication is too brief, too elaborate, or unresponsive. Performance discernment addresses how the assistant works with the user. Judge interaction against the user’s needs rather than a universal preference for brevity or detail.

When a response falls short, specify the problem, explain why it matters for the task, and give a concrete suggestion for improvement. Revise the relevant instructions or examples rather than relying only on a vague request to improve. A diagnosed defect can be translated into information the assistant can act on. Explaining the desired correction connects evaluation to the next useful instruction. Reconsider delegation or the tool when a communication correction does not address the underlying limitation.

Compare the desired and observed product, process, and interaction to choose the next move: clarify context, add a demonstration, adjust constraints or method, request alternatives, start a fresh conversation, or reconsider the tool and division of work. Reevaluate the result and retain human decisions about what to use. Different mismatches call for different interventions. Description and Discernment form a feedback loop, while some failures require a change in Delegation rather than another wording revision. Missing access differs from poor instructions, and a revised prompt still requires evaluation of its result.

Before selecting a service or sharing information with it, consider how it is built, who owns and may access the input data, privacy and security, affected people and other impacts, personal or professional values, and applicable organizational policies. Productive use alone does not settle whether sharing is appropriate. AI interaction has consequences beyond completing the immediate task. Creation diligence connects system and data choices to the people, responsibilities, and policies surrounding the work. Use the actual policy and data conditions; helpful output does not establish permission to share inputs.

Determine who needs to know about AI involvement, what role to disclose, how and when to communicate it, and how much detail fits the context. Be open and accurate about the actual contribution and meet the relevant personal, academic, creative, or professional expectations. Disclosure supports trust and enables affected people to understand AI’s role. Different settings and stakeholders can have different expectations, so a single stock disclosure is not sufficient for every situation. Use the relevant contextual expectations rather than inventing one universal disclosure requirement.

Before using or sharing AI-assisted work, perform the checks needed for that context, including accuracy, sources, bias, appropriateness, and usage rights. The human using or releasing the work remains responsible for the final output and its impact. AI can make mistakes, while the decision to rely on or release its contribution belongs to the person using it. Deployment diligence connects review with the ability to stand behind the final work. Disclosure does not replace checking, and AI involvement does not transfer accountability to the system.

Write a project-specific diligence statement identifying the AI systems used, their actual contributions, the review performed, responsibility for the output, and relevant contextual considerations. Describe completed checks truthfully; do not claim a review that did not occur. The statement makes the collaboration and review visible to the relevant audience. Its value depends on accurately describing the project rather than copying assurances that may not be true. Truthfully describing incomplete review does not itself make unfinished work ready for release.

For continued practice, identify specific strengths and areas for growth, choose development priorities, plan concrete activities and practice times, and specify how progress will be recognized. Revisit the plan as needs and AI capabilities change. A concrete plan connects continued practice to the learner’s own priorities as tasks and AI capabilities change.

For recurring tasks, maintain reusable prompt templates with places for changing context, notes about helpful Description and Discernment patterns, examples of successful outputs, and an accessible organization and update process. Variable fields and updates keep a reusable resource responsive to the actual task rather than freezing one successful interaction. For reuse, supply the new task’s variable information and evaluate the resulting output.

misconceptions.text: A fluent or confident answer is sufficient evidence that its facts and reasoning are correct.
A larger or more advanced model must answer this particular task correctly.
The language model normally answers by retrieving a fixed, verified response from a database.
Following examples in a conversation proves that the underlying model has been retrained.
A training cutoff means that current information is unavailable even when appropriate tools or documents are supplied.
A capable assistant automatically has access to private records or specialized tools.
Everything previously mentioned remains available throughout any conversation.
Repeating the same request must produce exactly the same answer.
Every task and model requires a detailed step-by-step or think-first instruction.
Asking for a rationale after an answer is equivalent to asking the assistant to consider the problem before producing it.
The most effective AI collaboration always delegates as much work as possible to AI.
Choosing an advanced AI system removes the need to clarify the goal and work involved.
One assistant is the best choice for every task and will remain so.
The assistant will infer the user’s unstated situation, requirements, and success criteria.
Description consists only of requesting a final product; the work approach and interaction cannot be specified.
Every useful prompt must contain several examples.
Any pair of examples is adequate, even if it fails to demonstrate the desired pattern or relevant variation.
The AI’s work process and the quality of its interaction with the user are the same dimension.
Repeating a vague request to improve supplies enough corrective feedback.
Better wording alone can solve a task that requires data or access the assistant does not have.
The same disclosure, audience, timing, and level of detail fit every use of AI.
If a service is useful for the task, sharing the input with it is appropriate.
The AI is responsible for errors in the final work, so the person using it need not stand behind it.
A diligence statement may claim thorough checking just because that assurance appears in a template.
